fields.Front: What problem does Inversion of Control (IoC) solve in application design?
fields.Back: It removes the responsibility of creating and wiring dependencies from application classes, delegating object creation and lifecycle management to a container (the Spring IoC container), reducing tight coupling between classes.
An object that is instantiated, assembled, and managed by the Spring IoC container (as opposed to being created directly with new by application code).

fields.Front: What is the difference between "singleton" and "prototype" bean scope in Spring?
fields.Back: Singleton: one shared instance per Spring container, reused for every injection point. Prototype: a brand-new instance is created every time the bean is requested/injected.

fields.Front: How do you code a class as a Spring REST controller that exposes a GET endpoint?
fields.Back:
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/eforms")
public class EFormController {
    private final EFormService service;
    public EFormController(EFormService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public EForm getForm(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return service.findById(id);
    }
}

fields.Front: What does @RestController combine, compared to plain @Controller?
fields.Back: @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody — every handler method's return value is serialized directly into the HTTP response body (e.g. as JSON) instead of being resolved to a view template.

fields.Front: Why annotate a class with @Service or @Repository instead of just @Component?
fields.Back: Both are specializations of @Component so they're still auto-detected as beans, but they add meaning: @Service marks business-logic classes; @Repository marks data-access classes and also enables Spring's exception translation, converting persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy.

fields.Front: Why is constructor injection generally preferred over field injection with @Autowired?
fields.Back: It makes dependencies explicit and lets fields be final/immutable, allows the class to be instantiated outside Spring (easier unit testing without a container), fails fast at startup if a dependency is missing, and avoids hidden circular-dependency issues.

fields.Front: In the ServiceOntario full-stack app (Spring Boot + React), which annotation exposes the JSON endpoints the React front-end calls?
fields.Back: @RestController (combined with @RequestMapping/@GetMapping/@PostMapping etc.) — handler methods return Java objects that Spring serializes to JSON for the React client to consume over HTTP.

fields.Front: How do you code idiomatic constructor injection for a Spring service (no Lombok)?
fields.Back:
@Service
public class EFormService {
    private final EFormRepository repository;

    public EFormService(EFormRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}

A mechanism (@EnableAutoConfiguration, pulled in by @SpringBootApplication) that automatically configures beans based on the classpath contents, existing beans, and property settings — e.g. adding a DataSource bean automatically once a JDBC driver is on the classpath.

fields.Front: What is a Spring Boot "starter" (e.g. spring-boot-starter-web)?
fields.Back: A curated dependency descriptor that bundles a set of version-compatible libraries for a use case (web, JPA, security, etc.), so you don't have to manage each transitive dependency and version yourself.

fields.Front: How do Spring profiles let you vary configuration between environments?
fields.Back: You define environment-specific property files (application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml) and/or annotate beans with @Profile("dev"); activating a profile via spring.profiles.active=prod makes Spring load only the matching config and beans.

fields.Front: How do you hook into bean initialization and cleanup using annotations?
fields.Back:
@Component
public class ConnectionPool {
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        // open connections
    }
    @PreDestroy
    public void cleanup() {
        // close connections
    }
}

fields.Front: What does @Transactional do when placed on a Spring service method?
fields.Back: Wraps the call in a proxy that starts a database transaction before the method executes and commits it on success, rolling it back automatically if an unchecked (RuntimeException) exception propagates out.

fields.Front: By default, does Spring's @Transactional roll back on checked exceptions?
fields.Back: No — by default it only rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) and Error, not checked exceptions, unless rollbackFor is explicitly specified.

fields.Front: How do you centrally handle exceptions thrown by any @RestController in a Spring Boot app?
fields.Back:
@ControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(EFormNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<String> handleNotFound(EFormNotFoundException ex) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .body(ex.getMessage());
    }
}

fields.Front: What is Spring Boot Actuator used for?
fields.Back: A set of production-ready endpoints (e.g. /actuator/health, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/info) for monitoring and managing a running application — health checks, metrics, environment info — without building that infrastructure yourself.

fields.Text: The default scope of a Spring bean is {{c1::singleton}} — only one shared instance is created per Spring container/application context and reused for every injection.
fields.Extra: Other scopes: prototype, request, session, application.

fields.Text: Spring Boot externalizes configuration in {{c1::application.yml}} (or application.properties), letting values like {{c2::server.port}} and datasource URLs live outside compiled code.
fields.Extra: YAML is a hierarchical alternative to the flat .properties format.

fields.Text: Spring bean lifecycle order: instantiate → inject dependencies → {{c1::@PostConstruct}} callback runs → bean is ready for use → {{c2::@PreDestroy}} callback runs on container shutdown.
